questions.question: Why do AI features need incident runbooks?
options: Because standard uptime monitoring already covers every way an assistant can degrade
Because support teams respond faster when each incident is handled case by case
Because most AI incidents resolve themselves once the provider rotates the model
Because model behavior, retrieval quality, tool calls, cost, and safety controls can fail
questions.explanation: AI operations covers quality, cost, safety, and tool behavior in addition to uptime. Without a runbook, support teams improvise and the business loses trust.

questions.question: A live assistant starts blocking valid work because a guardrail fires too often. Which operational signal is this?
options: A cost spike - each blocked request is retried, which multiplies the tokens consumed
A safety alert - the guardrail is firing on legitimate requests and needs triage
Quality drift - the model's answers have degraded slowly since the last release
A tool failure - the integration behind the guardrail stopped returning a verdict
questions.explanation: The lesson lists a safety alert as one of four operational signals, alongside quality drift, cost spikes, and tool failure. A guardrail blocking valid work is an incident to triage, not a tuning detail.

questions.question: What does the Python artifact produce?
options: A production monitoring platform that watches quality, cost, and tool health
A root cause determined automatically from the alert and the recent changes
A service management process that replaces the existing incident workflow
A ranked incident triage plan with matched controls and rationale
questions.explanation: The artifact helps plan incident response controls by ranking findings and matching each to a control. It extends service management rather than replacing it.

questions.question: Which control belongs to this lesson?
options: A rollback path that returns the feature to a known-good state during containment
An alert threshold set high enough that routine quality variation stays quiet
A shared support inbox with no named owner, so whoever is free picks it up
A resolution note filed instead of a postmortem once the incident is closed
questions.explanation: Rollback paths help contain AI feature incidents. Runbooks, named escalation owners, and postmortems are the other controls this lesson teaches.

questions.question: When should an AI incident trigger escalation?
options: Only when the outage is visible on the status page for external customers
Only when the failure is in infrastructure rather than in model behavior
When impact, uncertainty, and operational risk signals are high enough
Only when the on-call engineer cannot reproduce the problem within an hour
questions.explanation: High-impact operational issues need clear escalation, and every AI feature needs a named escalation owner. AI incidents are not only uptime incidents.

questions.question: What should a postmortem update after an AI incident?
options: Only the customer status page and the note sent to affected stakeholders
Only the on-call rota, so the next incident reaches a different engineer
Evals, prompts, tools, controls, and the runbook the team followed
Only the alert threshold that fired, since the rest of the stack held up
questions.explanation: Postmortems should improve the operating system around the AI feature: evals, prompts, tools, controls, and runbooks.
